check.q: Why are sodium and potassium stored under kerosene?
options: Because they react vigorously with air and moisture
check.why: Sodium and potassium react so vigorously with oxygen and water vapour that they can catch fire, so they are kept under kerosene to exclude air.

sections.md:
**Why do elements react?** Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar…) have a **complete outer shell** (octet, or duplet for He) and are unreactive. Other atoms react to reach such a stable configuration by **losing, gaining or sharing** electrons.

**Sodium chloride:** Na (2, 8, 1) loses one electron → Na⁺ (2, 8). Cl (2, 8, 7) gains it → Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8). The oppositely charged ions attract: an **ionic** (electrovalent) bond.

**Magnesium chloride:** Mg (2, 8, 2) gives one electron each to two Cl atoms → Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ → MgCl₂.

**Electron-dot structures:** show only valence electrons as dots or crosses, e.g. Na· + ·Cl (with seven dots) → [Na]⁺ [Cl with eight dots]⁻.

### 3.3.1 Properties of ionic compounds (Activity 3.13)
| Property | Reason |
|---|---|
| Solid, hard, brittle | strong attraction between ions in a lattice; layers shatter under pressure |
| High melting and boiling points (NaCl melts at 1074 K) | lots of energy needed to overcome strong forces |
| Soluble in water, insoluble in kerosene/petrol | water molecules surround and separate ions |
| Conduct electricity when **molten or dissolved**, not as solids | ions are free to move only in liquid or solution |

> Did you know? The salt pans of Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu produce millions of tonnes of salt a year — each grain a lattice of trillions of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in perfect alternation.

check.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten NaCl does, because:
options: ions can move only in the molten state
check.why: In the solid, ions are locked in a rigid lattice; melting frees them to move and carry charge.

sections.md:
The Earth’s crust is the main source; seawater has soluble salts like NaCl and MgCl₂. Naturally occurring compounds are **minerals**; minerals from which a metal can be extracted profitably are **ores**.

**Gold, silver, platinum, copper** (low reactivity) are found **free** (native). K to Al are never free. Middle metals occur as oxides, sulphides or carbonates.

### 3.4.1 Enrichment
Ores contain earthy impurities called **gangue**. These are removed first by physical/chemical methods based on differences in properties.

### 3.4.2 Extraction by reactivity
| Position | Method | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Low** (Hg, Cu) | heating alone | 2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂; 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂. Copper: 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂; 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂ |
| **Middle** (Zn, Fe, Pb) | convert to oxide, then reduce with carbon | **Roasting** (sulphide in excess air): 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. **Calcination** (carbonate, limited air): ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. Reduction: ZnO + C → Zn + CO |
| **High** (Na, Mg, Ca, Al) | electrolysis of molten chlorides/oxides | Molten NaCl: Na at cathode, Cl₂ at anode. Aluminium from Al₂O₃ |

**Thermite reaction:** a highly reactive metal reduces a less reactive metal’s oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ + heat. So much heat is released that iron comes out **molten** — used to **join railway tracks** and repair cracked machine parts.

### 3.4.3 Refining
**Electrolytic refining** (Cu, Zn, Sn, Ni, Ag, Au): impure metal = **anode**, a thin strip of pure metal = **cathode**, a solution of its salt = electrolyte. Pure metal deposits on the cathode; soluble impurities stay in solution; insoluble ones settle below the anode as **anode mud**.

sections.md:
**Corrosion examples:** silver turns black (silver sulphide, from sulphur in air); copper gains a green coat (basic copper carbonate, from moist CO₂); iron rusts (reddish-brown hydrated iron(III) oxide).

**Activity 3.14 — what makes iron rust?** Three test tubes with clean iron nails:
- A: nails in ordinary tap water, open to air → **rust**.
- B: nails in boiled distilled water with a layer of oil on top (no air) → **no rust**.
- C: nails with anhydrous calcium chloride (dry air, no moisture) → **no rust**.
Conclusion: **both air (oxygen) and water** are needed for rusting.

### 3.5.1 Prevention
- Painting, oiling, greasing.
- **Galvanising:** coating iron/steel with **zinc**. Even if the zinc is scratched, the iron is protected, because zinc is more reactive and corrodes first.
- Chrome plating, anodising, making **alloys**.

### Alloys
A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, made by melting and mixing. Pure iron is very soft and stretches; with 0.05% carbon it becomes hard and strong **steel**.
| Alloy | Composition | Use / property |
|---|---|---|
| Stainless steel | iron + nickel + chromium | hard, doesn’t rust — utensils |
| Brass | copper + zinc | taps, instruments |
| Bronze | copper + tin | statues, bells |
| Solder | lead + tin | low melting point — welding electrical wires |
| Amalgam | mercury + another metal | — |
| 22-carat gold | 22 parts gold + 2 parts copper/silver | harder than 24-carat for jewellery |

Alloys usually have **lower electrical conductivity** and **lower melting points** than the pure metals.

**Iron pillar of Delhi:** made about 1,600 years ago (in the Gupta period) and over 7 m tall, it has resisted rusting remarkably well. Studies credit the high phosphorus content of the ancient wrought iron, which helps form a protective surface film.

check.q: In the rusting experiment, why does the nail in boiled water with oil on top not rust?
options: Oil and boiling keep out dissolved air (oxygen)
check.why: Boiling removes dissolved air and the oil layer stops air re-dissolving, so without oxygen the iron cannot rust.

rd-school-c10-science-a.ch4-carbon-and-i.title: Carbon and its Compounds
rd-school-c10-science-a.ch4-carbon-and-i.subtitle: One element, millions of compounds: how carbon builds fuels, foods, plastics — and you

sections.md:
Your cotton shirt, the chapati at lunch, the petrol in a scooter, the plastic of your pen, the DNA in your cells, the diamond in a ring — all are built around one element: **carbon**. The earth's crust holds only about 0.02% carbon (as carbonates, coal, petroleum), and the atmosphere about 0.03% carbon dioxide. Yet more compounds of carbon are known than of all other elements put together — several million!

Why? To answer, we must look at the **bonds** carbon makes.

Recall from Chapter 3 that ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten. Most carbon compounds are the opposite: low melting and boiling points, and they are **poor conductors** of electricity. This tells us the bonds in them do not produce ions.

Carbon has atomic number 6: electronic configuration **2, 4**. To get a noble-gas octet it would have to gain 4 electrons (C⁴⁻) or lose 4 (C⁴⁺). Both are hard — six protons cannot hold ten electrons easily, and removing four electrons needs a lot of energy. So carbon **shares** its valence electrons with other atoms. A bond formed by sharing a pair of electrons is a **covalent bond**.

### Simple examples
- **Hydrogen, H₂**: each H shares its one electron; both get a helium-like duplet. A single bond: H–H.
- **Oxygen, O₂**: each O (2, 6) shares two electrons — a **double bond**, O=O.
- **Nitrogen, N₂**: each N (2, 5) shares three — a **triple bond**, N≡N.
- **Water, H₂O**: oxygen shares one electron with each of two H atoms.
- **Methane, CH₄**: carbon shares its four electrons with four H atoms. Valency of carbon = 4 (**tetravalent**). Methane is the main part of natural gas, CNG and biogas.

Covalent compounds have strong bonds **within** molecules but weak forces **between** molecules — hence low melting and boiling points. No ions — so they do not conduct electricity.

### Allotropes of carbon
The same element in different physical forms:
- **Diamond**: each C bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network — hardest natural substance, does not conduct.
- **Graphite**: each C bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers; layers slide (good lubricant, pencil 'lead'); one electron per C is free, so graphite **conducts**.
- **Fullerenes**: C-60 is a football-shaped cage named after architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes it resembles.

check.q: Why do most carbon compounds not conduct electricity?
options: Their bonding is covalent so no ions are formed
They have very high melting points
check.why: Covalent compounds share electrons and do not form ions, so there are no charged particles to carry current.

sections.h: Why carbon makes so many compounds
sections.md:
Two special properties:

1. **Catenation** — carbon atoms link to other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings. Silicon shows a little catenation (up to about 7–8 atoms) but those compounds are very reactive; C–C bonds are very strong and stable.
2. **Tetravalency** — with four bonds per atom, carbon can bond with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many others, and with other carbons. Its small size lets the nucleus hold shared pairs tightly, making strong bonds.

Carbon compounds were once called **organic compounds** because they were thought to come only from living things. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from ammonium cyanate in the laboratory, ending that idea — but the name stayed.

### Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are **hydrocarbons**.
- **Alkanes** (single bonds, saturated): CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀.
- **Alkenes** (one C=C double bond, unsaturated): CₙH₂ₙ — ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆.
- **Alkynes** (one C≡C triple bond, unsaturated): CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — ethyne C₂H₂, propyne C₃H₄.

Carbon may also form **rings**: cyclohexane C₆H₁₂; benzene C₆H₆ has alternating double bonds.

### Isomers
Butane C₄H₁₀ can be a straight chain (n-butane) or branched (isobutane, 2-methylpropane). Same molecular formula, different structures = **structural isomers**.

### Functional groups
An atom or group replacing hydrogen in a hydrocarbon gives the compound its characteristic properties.

| Group | Formula | Suffix/prefix | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halo | –Cl, –Br | chloro-, bromo- | chloropropane |
| Alcohol | –OH | -ol | propanol |
| Aldehyde | –CHO | -al | propanal |
| Ketone | >C=O | -one | propanone |
| Carboxylic acid | –COOH | -oic acid | propanoic acid |

### Homologous series
A series of compounds with the same functional group, where each member differs from the next by **–CH₂–** (a mass of 14 u). CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH form the alcohol series. Physical properties (melting point, boiling point) change gradually with mass; chemical properties stay similar.

### Naming (nomenclature)
1. Find the number of carbons: 1 meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex.
2. Add the functional group as prefix or suffix (drop the final 'e' if the suffix begins with a vowel): propane → propanone.
3. If unsaturated, use -ene / -yne.

sections.md:
### Combustion
Carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give CO₂, heat and light:
- C + O₂ → CO₂ + heat and light
- CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat and light
- CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O + heat and light

Saturated hydrocarbons usually burn with a clean **blue flame**; unsaturated ones give a **yellow, sooty flame**. If the air holes of a gas stove are blocked, insufficient oxygen causes incomplete burning and a yellow flame that blackens the bottom of vessels. Coal and petroleum also contain nitrogen and sulphur, so burning them gives oxides that cause acid rain. A candle flame is yellow because unburnt carbon particles glow; burning gives a flame only for substances that vaporise.

### Oxidation
Alkaline **potassium permanganate** or acidified **potassium dichromate** are **oxidising agents** that convert alcohols to acids: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOH (with alkaline KMnO₄ + heat). The purple colour of KMnO₄ disappears as it is used up.

### Addition reaction
Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts like **nickel** or palladium. This is how vegetable oils (unsaturated, with long chains) are **hydrogenated** to make vanaspati ghee. Animal fats are mostly saturated and are considered less healthy; vegetable oils with unsaturated fatty acids are generally healthier choices.

### Substitution reaction
Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive, but in **sunlight** chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (in sunlight). Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄.

sections.h: Two important compounds: ethanol and ethanoic acid
sections.md:
### Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
Commonly called alcohol; the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks; a good solvent used in medicines like tincture iodine and cough syrups. Liquid at room temperature, soluble in water in all proportions. Drinking even small amounts has harmful effects; consuming it causes many health problems. Ethanol made unfit to drink by adding poisonous methanol and a blue dye is **denatured alcohol** — methanol in drinks can cause blindness and death.

**Reactions:**
- With sodium: 2Na + 2CH₃CH₂OH → 2CH₃CH₂ONa (sodium ethoxide) + H₂.
- With hot concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K (dehydration): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Conc. H₂SO₄ is the dehydrating agent.

**As a fuel:** sugarcane is efficient at turning sunlight into chemical energy; its molasses is fermented to ethanol. Ethanol mixed with petrol (blended fuel) burns cleanly — India's ethanol-blending programme aims to reduce oil imports.

### Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH)
Acetic acid; a 5–8% solution in water is **vinegar**, a preservative in pickles. Pure ethanoic acid freezes at 290 K, so in cold weather it looks like ice — hence **glacial acetic acid**. It is a **weak acid** compared to HCl.

**Reactions:**
- **Esterification**: with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst gives a sweet-smelling **ester**: CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. Esters are used in perfumes and flavours.
- **Saponification**: ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt of the acid. Making soap is saponification.
- With a base: NaOH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
- With carbonates: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂; with NaHCO₃ similarly.
keyTerms: esterification — acid + alcohol → ester + water
saponification — alkaline hydrolysis of ester, makes soap
glacial acetic acid — pure ethanoic acid that freezes in winter

check.q: Which gas is evolved when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate?
check.why: Acids react with hydrogen carbonates to give salt, water and carbon dioxide.

sections.md:
Most dirt is oily and does not dissolve in water. A **soap** molecule is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid. It has two ends:

- an **ionic end** that is **hydrophilic** (water-loving) — dissolves in water;
- a long **carbon chain** that is **hydrophobic** (water-hating) — dissolves in oil.

In water, soap molecules gather into clusters called **micelles**: the hydrocarbon tails point inward, trapping oily dirt at the centre, while the ionic heads face outward into the water. The micelle stays suspended in water like a colloid; rinsing washes it away with the dirt. Soap micelles scatter light, so a soap solution looks cloudy.

### The problem of hard water
Bathing with water from some wells or borewells, you need a lot of soap and a white, sticky **scum** forms. **Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts, which react with soap to form insoluble scum — wasting soap.

**Detergents** are sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions, with long hydrocarbon chains. Their charged ends do **not** form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work well even in hard water. They are used in shampoos and clothes-cleaning products. (Some older detergents were not biodegradable, causing foam in rivers.)

> Hook: Your *roti*, your cotton kurta, the LPG in your kitchen, the medicine in your cupboard and the DNA in your cells all have one thing in common — carbon. Earth’s crust has only about 0.02% carbon (as minerals) and the atmosphere about 0.03% CO₂, yet millions of carbon compounds are known — more than those of all other elements put together. Why?

check.q: Approximately what share of the Earth’s crust is carbon (as minerals)?
check.why: Carbon makes up only about 0.02% of the crust, yet it forms more compounds than all other elements combined.

sections.md:
Carbon (atomic number 6) has configuration **2, 4**. To get an octet it would have to gain 4 electrons (C⁴⁻ — hard for 6 protons to hold 10 electrons) or lose 4 (C⁴⁺ — needs huge energy). So carbon **shares** its valence electrons — forming **covalent bonds**.

| Molecule | Bond | How |
|---|---|---|
| H₂ | single (H–H) | each H shares 1 electron → duplet |
| Cl₂ | single | each Cl shares 1 → octet |
| O₂ | **double** (O=O) | each O shares 2 |
| N₂ | **triple** (N≡N) | each N shares 3 |
| H₂O | two single | O shares with 2 H |
| CH₄ (methane) | four single | C shares one with each of 4 H |
| CO₂ | two double (O=C=O) | — |

Methane is the main gas in **CNG and biogas**.

**Properties of covalent compounds:** generally **low melting and boiling points** (weak intermolecular forces), and **poor conductors** of electricity (no ions). Compare: methane boils at about 111 K; NaCl melts at 1074 K.

### Allotropes of carbon
- **Diamond:** each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D network — the hardest natural substance, does not conduct.
- **Graphite:** each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers, layers held weakly — slippery (lubricant, pencil ‘lead’), **conducts** electricity.
- **Fullerenes:** C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene) shaped like a football — named after architect Buckminster Fuller’s geodesic domes.

Diamonds can be made by subjecting pure carbon to very high pressure and temperature.

check.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity while diamond does not?
options: Each carbon in graphite uses only 3 electrons for bonding, leaving mobile electrons
check.why: In graphite each carbon bonds to three others, so one electron per atom is free to move through the layers and carry current.

sections.md:
Two special properties:
1. **Catenation** — carbon bonds with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings. No other element does this as well (silicon forms chains of only 7–8 atoms, and they are reactive).
2. **Tetravalency** — four bonds allow carbon to bond with C, H, O, N, S, Cl and more. Carbon’s **small size** makes these bonds strong, so compounds are stable.

### 4.2.1 Saturated vs unsaturated
- **Saturated** (single bonds only): **alkanes**, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈.
- **Unsaturated** (double or triple bonds): **alkenes** CₙH₂ₙ (ethene C₂H₄, H₂C=CH₂) and **alkynes** CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne C₂H₂, HC≡CH).

**Hydrocarbons** contain only C and H.

### 4.2.2 Chains, branches and rings
- Butane C₄H₁₀ can be straight (n-butane) or branched (isobutane) — same formula, different structure: **structural isomers**.
- Cyclohexane C₆H₁₂ — a ring of single bonds.
- **Benzene C₆H₆** — a ring with alternating double bonds.

### 4.2.3 Functional groups (heteroatoms)
An atom or group that gives a compound its characteristic properties, whatever the chain length.
| Group | Formula | Name ending | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Halo | –Cl, –Br | prefix chloro/bromo | chloropropane |
| Alcohol | –OH | -ol | propanol |
| Aldehyde | –CHO | -al | propanal |
| Ketone | >C=O | -one | propanone |
| Carboxylic acid | –COOH | -oic acid | propanoic acid |

### 4.2.4 Homologous series
Compounds with the same functional group, differing by **–CH₂–** (14 u). E.g. CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH, C₄H₉OH. Members have **similar chemical properties**, while physical properties (melting/boiling point, solubility) **change gradually** with molecular mass.

### 4.2.5 Naming (IUPAC)
1. Count carbons → stem: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6).
2. Add the functional-group ending (replacing the final ‘e’ of the alkane where needed): propane → propanol, propanal, propanone, propanoic acid; ethene, ethyne for double/triple bonds.
3. Halogens as prefixes: bromoethane.

Examples: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl — 1-chloropropane; CH₃COCH₃ — propanone; HCHO — methanal; C₂H₅OH — ethanol.

check.q: What is the difference in molecular mass between consecutive members of a homologous series?
check.why: Successive members differ by a CH₂ unit, whose mass is 12 + 2 = 14 u.

sections.md:
### 4.3.1 Combustion
Carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen giving CO₂, heat and light.
C + O₂ → CO₂; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
- **Saturated** hydrocarbons usually burn with a **clean blue flame**.
- **Unsaturated** ones give a **yellow, sooty flame** (incomplete combustion).
- A cooking pot turning black at the base means air holes of the stove are blocked — fuel is wasted. Clean them!
- Burning fossil fuels produces oxides of sulphur and nitrogen — major pollutants.
- **Flame vs glow:** substances that vaporise on burning give flames; charcoal just glows.

### 4.3.2 Oxidation
Alcohols → carboxylic acids using **oxidising agents** like alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate:
CH₃CH₂OH → (alk. KMnO₄ + heat) → CH₃COOH. The purple colour of KMnO₄ disappears as it is used up.

### 4.3.3 Addition
Unsaturated compounds add hydrogen in the presence of a **catalyst** (nickel or palladium): R₂C=CR₂ + H₂ → R₂CH–CHR₂. This **hydrogenation** turns **vegetable oils** (unsaturated, long chains) into **vanaspati ghee** (saturated fats). Health note: oils with unsaturated fatty acids are generally considered healthier; saturated fats in excess are linked to heart disease — follow your doctor’s advice.

### 4.3.4 Substitution
Saturated hydrocarbons are quite unreactive but, in **sunlight**, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one:
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (and further products CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄).

> Did you know? A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction without itself being used up — the nickel in an oil-hardening factory can be reused many times.

check.q: Why does a gas stove flame turn yellow and the vessel bottom black?
options: Incomplete combustion due to insufficient air
check.why: Blocked air holes limit oxygen, so the fuel burns incompletely, giving a sooty yellow flame and carbon deposits.

sections.md:
### 4.4.1 Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
A colourless liquid at room temperature, soluble in water in all proportions; the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks and used in tincture iodine, cough syrups and tonics; a good solvent.
- **Health note:** even small amounts cause drunkenness; regular consumption seriously harms health. **Methanol** (CH₃OH) is extremely poisonous — even small quantities can cause blindness or death. Industrial alcohol is **denatured** by adding methanol, and a blue dye is added to make it identifiable.
- **Reaction with sodium:** 2Na + 2CH₃CH₂OH → 2CH₃CH₂ONa (sodium ethoxide) + H₂. (Activity: hydrogen evolved — test with a burning splinter.)
- **Dehydration:** heating with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives **ethene**: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as a dehydrating agent.
- **Ethanol as fuel:** sugarcane juice can be fermented to ethanol, a clean fuel. India blends ethanol into petrol (ethanol-blended petrol programme).

### 4.4.2 Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH, acetic acid)
- **Vinegar** is a 5–8% solution in water, used as a preservative in pickles.
- Pure ethanoic acid freezes at 290 K, so it often freezes in cold climates — hence **glacial acetic acid**.
- It is a **weak acid** (only partly ionised).
- **Esterification:** ethanoic acid + ethanol with a little concentrated H₂SO₄ (catalyst), warmed → **ester** (ethyl ethanoate), sweet-smelling, used in perfumes and flavours: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
- **Saponification:** ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt of the acid: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → C₂H₅OH + CH₃COONa. This is how **soap** is made from fats.
- **With a base:** NaOH + CH₃COOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O.
- **With carbonates:** 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂; CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.

check.q: Which test distinguishes ethanoic acid from ethanol?
options: Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate — the acid gives CO₂ brisk effervescence
check.why: Ethanoic acid reacts with NaHCO₃ to release CO₂ (fizzing, turns lime water milky); ethanol does not.

sections.md:
**Soap** molecules are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Each has two ends:
- an **ionic, hydrophilic** head (–COO⁻Na⁺) that dissolves in water;
- a long **hydrocarbon, hydrophobic** tail that dissolves in oil.

**Micelles:** in water, soap molecules arrange in clusters with tails pointing inward (into the oily dirt) and heads outward (towards water). The oily dirt is trapped in the centre of the **micelle**, which stays suspended in water and is rinsed away. Micelles scatter light, so soap solution looks cloudy.

**Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with them to form an insoluble **scum**, wasting soap. (Activity: shake soap with distilled water and with hard water — foam forms easily in distilled water; scum forms in hard water.)

**Detergents** are usually ammonium or sulphonate salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Their charged ends **don’t form insoluble precipitates** with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so they work in hard water. They are used in shampoos and laundry products.

| Soap | Detergent |
|---|---|
| Na/K salt of long-chain fatty acid | ammonium or sulphonate salt |
| Forms scum in hard water | works in hard water |
| Biodegradable | many are not easily biodegradable |

> Did you know? Before soap became common, many Indian households washed clothes with *ritha* (soapnut) — its natural saponins form micelles just like soap.

rd-school-c10-science-a.ch5-life-process.title: Life Processes
rd-school-c10-science-a.ch5-life-process.subtitle: Nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion — the round-the-clock maintenance work that keeps you alive

sections.h: What does it mean to be alive?
sections.md:
A dog running is obviously alive. A sleeping cow chewing cud — alive. But what about a tree standing perfectly still, or a person in deep sleep? We see no movement, yet we know they are alive. The real sign of life is invisible: **molecular movement**. Inside every cell, molecules are constantly being broken down and built up to repair and maintain the body's organised structures. Living things are highly ordered, and the environment keeps trying to disorder them. Maintenance needs energy — and that is the job of **life processes**: the processes that together perform maintenance.

Energy comes from outside, as **food**. Since life on earth is carbon-based, most food is carbon-based. Getting food in is **nutrition**. Breaking it down for energy — usually using oxygen — is **respiration**. In single-celled organisms the whole surface touches the environment, so simple diffusion is enough. In large multicellular organisms like us, special tissues are needed to take in food and oxygen, a **transport** system to carry them around, and a way to remove harmful wastes — **excretion**.

This chapter covers all four: nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion.
keyTerms: life processes — processes that maintain living organisms
nutrition — taking in and using food
respiration — releasing energy from food

sections.md:
Organisms that make their own food from simple inorganic materials (CO₂ and water) using sunlight are **autotrophs** — green plants and some bacteria. Organisms that depend on others are **heterotrophs** — animals, fungi.

### Photosynthesis
6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O  (sunlight, chlorophyll)

Three events happen:
1. Absorption of light energy by **chlorophyll**.
2. Conversion of light energy to chemical energy and **splitting of water** into hydrogen and oxygen.
3. **Reduction of CO₂** to carbohydrates.

These need not happen one after another immediately. Desert plants open their stomata at night, store CO₂ as an intermediate, and use it in daytime when light is available. The glucose made is stored as **starch**.

In a leaf cross-section, green dots called **chloroplasts** contain chlorophyll. Gases are exchanged through tiny pores, the **stomata**, each surrounded by two **guard cells** that swell (pore opens) when water flows in and shrink (pore closes) when they lose water. Plants close stomata when they do not need CO₂, to save water.

Plants also take nitrogen (as nitrates/nitrites from soil, or via bacteria), phosphorus, iron and magnesium from soil for proteins and other compounds.

**Experiments**: (1) A **variegated leaf** (green and white patches) kept in light, then tested with iodine, turns blue-black only in the green parts — chlorophyll is needed. (2) A potted plant kept in the dark for three days (to use up starch) and a leaf enclosed with potassium hydroxide (which absorbs CO₂) shows no starch — CO₂ is needed.

### How other organisms get food
Heterotrophs differ in how they obtain and break down food. Some break food down **outside** the body and absorb it (bread mould, yeast, mushrooms — **saprotrophs**). Others take whole food in and digest it inside (cows, humans). Some live on or in another organism and take nutrition from it without killing it — **parasites** like cuscuta (amar-bel), ticks, lice, leeches and tapeworms.

**Amoeba** takes in food by sending out finger-like **pseudopodia** that surround the particle and form a **food vacuole**; complex substances are broken down there and diffuse into the cytoplasm; undigested matter is thrown out at the surface. **Paramoecium** has a definite shape and uses **cilia** to move food to a specific spot.

sections.md:
The **alimentary canal** is a long tube from mouth to anus with regions specialised for different jobs.

- **Mouth**: teeth chew food into small pieces; the tongue mixes it. **Salivary glands** release saliva containing the enzyme **salivary amylase**, which breaks starch into sugar (maltose). Chew a piece of roti for a while and it tastes sweet!
- **Oesophagus** (food pipe): rhythmic contractions of muscles — **peristalsis** — push food down. Peristalsis occurs along the whole gut.
- **Stomach**: a large organ that expands with food. Gastric glands release **hydrochloric acid** (creates an acidic medium and kills germs), **pepsin** (protein-digesting enzyme) and **mucus** (protects the stomach lining from acid). Too much acid causes acidity. A **sphincter muscle** regulates exit into the small intestine.
- **Small intestine**: the longest part, highly coiled. Herbivores eating grass have a longer small intestine to digest cellulose; carnivores like tigers have shorter ones. It receives **bile** from the **liver** — bile is alkaline, neutralising stomach acid so pancreatic enzymes can act, and it breaks large fat globules into smaller ones (**emulsification**). The **pancreas** secretes **pancreatic juice** with **trypsin** (proteins) and **lipase** (emulsified fats). Glands in the intestinal wall secrete **intestinal juice**, converting proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates to glucose and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.
- **Absorption**: the inner lining has millions of finger-like **villi**, which greatly increase surface area and are richly supplied with blood vessels that take digested food to every cell.
- **Large intestine**: more villi absorb water; the rest is removed through the anus, regulated by the anal sphincter.

check.q: What is the function of villi in the small intestine?
options: Increase surface area for absorption of digested food
check.why: Villi are finger-like projections with blood vessels that greatly enlarge the absorbing surface.

sections.md:
Glucose (6 carbons) is first broken into **pyruvate** (3 carbons) in the **cytoplasm**. What happens next depends on the organism:

- **Anaerobic (no oxygen), in yeast**: pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ + energy (fermentation).
- **Lack of oxygen in our muscles** (during a sprint): pyruvate → **lactic acid** + energy. Build-up of lactic acid causes **muscle cramps**.
- **Aerobic (with oxygen), in mitochondria**: pyruvate → CO₂ + H₂O + much more energy.

Aerobic respiration releases far more energy. The energy is stored as **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate), the **energy currency** of the cell. When ATP is broken down, a fixed amount of energy is released, driving muscle contraction, protein building, nerve impulses and more.

### Breathing in plants
Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels (in stems) by diffusion. At night they only release CO₂; during the day, the CO₂ from respiration is used in photosynthesis and oxygen is released.

### Breathing in animals
Aquatic animals take oxygen dissolved in water through **gills**. Since there is much less dissolved oxygen in water than in air, fish breathe much faster than land animals.

### Human respiratory system
Air enters through the **nostrils**, where fine hairs and mucus filter dust. It passes through the **throat** and **trachea** (wind-pipe), which has **rings of cartilage** so it does not collapse. In the lungs the passage divides into **bronchi**, then **bronchioles**, ending in balloon-like **alveoli**. Alveoli give a huge surface area — spread out, all the alveoli would cover about 80 m². Their walls have a network of blood vessels where oxygen diffuses into blood and CO₂ comes out.

When we breathe in, ribs lift and the **diaphragm** flattens, enlarging the chest cavity — air rushes in. The lungs always hold a residual volume of air, so there is enough time for gas exchange. **Haemoglobin**, a respiratory pigment in red blood cells, has a very high affinity for oxygen and carries it; CO₂ is more soluble and is carried mostly dissolved in blood.

check.q: Muscle cramps after a hard sprint are caused by:
options: Build-up of lactic acid due to lack of oxygen
check.why: When oxygen runs short, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactic acid, whose accumulation causes cramps.

sections.md:
**Blood** is a fluid connective tissue: liquid **plasma** carries food, CO₂ and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form; **red blood cells** carry oxygen; **white blood cells** fight disease; **platelets** help clotting.

### The heart
A muscular organ about the size of your fist with **four chambers**: two upper **atria** and two lower **ventricles**. Since oxygenated and deoxygenated blood must not mix, the heart is divided by a wall.

- Oxygen-rich blood from the **lungs** enters the thin-walled **left atrium** (via pulmonary veins), which contracts and sends it to the **left ventricle**. The left ventricle, with the thickest walls, pumps it to the **body** through the **aorta**.
- Deoxygenated blood from the body arrives in the **right atrium** (via vena cava), goes to the **right ventricle**, which pumps it to the **lungs** via the pulmonary artery.
- **Valves** prevent backflow when atria or ventricles contract.

Blood passes through the heart twice in each cycle — **double circulation** — keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood fully separate. This efficient oxygen supply suits birds and mammals, which need lots of energy to keep a constant body temperature. Amphibians and many reptiles have three-chambered hearts with some mixing; fish have two chambers and single circulation.

### Blood vessels
- **Arteries** carry blood **away** from the heart; thick, elastic walls because blood is under high pressure.
- **Veins** carry blood **to** the heart; thinner walls and valves to keep flow in one direction.
- **Capillaries** are one cell thick; exchange of materials happens through their walls.

**Blood pressure** is the force of blood on vessel walls. Normal is about 120/80 mm of Hg — 120 is **systolic** (ventricles contracting), 80 **diastolic** (relaxing). It is measured with a **sphygmomanometer**. High blood pressure (hypertension) can rupture arteries.

**Platelets** plug leaks when we are injured, forming a clot. **Lymph** (tissue fluid) — similar to plasma but colourless with less protein — drains through lymphatic vessels, carries digested fat from the intestine and returns extra fluid to blood.

### Transport in plants
Plants have low energy needs and move slowly, so their transport is slower.
- **Xylem** carries **water and minerals** from roots up. Root cells take up ions, creating a concentration difference so water moves in (**root pressure**, important at night). In the day, **transpiration** — loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata — creates a suction pull that draws water up, and also helps regulate temperature.
- **Phloem** carries food (sucrose, amino acids) — **translocation** — up and down, using energy from ATP to load sucrose; the resulting osmotic pressure pushes material to where it is needed. In spring, stored sugar from roots and stems moves to the buds.

check.q: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall?
options: It pumps blood to the whole body under high pressure
It receives blood from the lungs
check.why: The left ventricle must push oxygenated blood through the aorta to every part of the body, needing powerful muscle.

sections.md:
Removing harmful metabolic wastes — especially nitrogenous wastes like **urea** and **uric acid** — is **excretion**.

### Human excretory system
A pair of **kidneys**, a pair of **ureters**, a **urinary bladder** and a **urethra**. Kidneys sit in the abdomen on either side of the backbone. Each kidney has about a million filtering units called **nephrons**. In each nephron:

1. Blood enters a cluster of very thin-walled capillaries, the **glomerulus**, inside a cup-shaped **Bowman's capsule**, which collects the filtrate.
2. The filtrate — water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea — passes along the **tubule**, where useful substances (glucose, amino acids, salts, a major amount of water) are **selectively reabsorbed**. How much water is reabsorbed depends on how much extra water the body has and how much waste must be dissolved.
3. What remains is **urine**, which goes via collecting ducts to the ureter, is stored in the bladder, and released through the urethra under nervous control.

The kidneys filter about 180 litres of filtrate every day, yet only about 1–2 litres of urine are produced — the rest is reabsorbed.

### Artificial kidney (haemodialysis)
If kidneys fail due to infection, injury or restricted blood flow, poisonous wastes accumulate. An artificial kidney passes blood through long tubes with semi-permeable walls suspended in **dialysing fluid** that has the same osmotic pressure as blood but no nitrogenous wastes. Wastes diffuse out; purified blood returns. Unlike a real kidney, there is no reabsorption. Kidney transplants, usually from a close relative, are another option.

### Excretion in plants
Plants get rid of excess water by transpiration and of oxygen by diffusion. Other wastes are stored in **cellular vacuoles**, in leaves that later fall off, or as **resins and gums** in old xylem. Some wastes are released into the soil.

glomerulus — capillary knot inside Bowman's capsule
dialysis — artificial filtering of blood

check.q: Which is NOT reabsorbed in the tubules of a healthy nephron in large amounts?
check.why: Urea is a waste and stays in the filtrate to leave as urine, whereas glucose, amino acids and much water are reabsorbed.

summary: Life processes — nutrition, respiration, transport, excretion — maintain living systems.
Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis; heterotrophs depend on others.
Photosynthesis: light absorption, water splitting, CO₂ reduction; needs chlorophyll, CO₂, light, water.
Stomata, controlled by guard cells, exchange gases and lose water.
Human digestion: amylase (mouth), HCl and pepsin (stomach), bile, trypsin, lipase, intestinal juice.
Villi absorb digested food; large intestine absorbs water.
Glucose → pyruvate in cytoplasm; then ethanol + CO₂ (yeast), lactic acid (muscles), or CO₂ + H₂O in mitochondria.
ATP is the cell's energy currency.
Alveoli give a huge surface for gas exchange; haemoglobin carries oxygen.
The four-chambered heart gives double circulation.
Arteries carry blood away under high pressure; veins have valves; capillaries exchange materials.
Xylem carries water (transpiration pull, root pressure); phloem translocates food using ATP.
Nephrons filter blood; reabsorption leaves urine; dialysis replaces failed kidneys.
Plants excrete via transpiration, falling leaves, resins and gums.

rd-school-c10-science-a.ch5-life-process.subtitle: Every section and activity of the chapter, from a stoma opening at dawn to a nephron filtering your blood

sections.h: Map of the chapter: what are life processes?
sections.md:
| NCERT section | Ideas |
|---|---|
| 5.1 What are life processes? | Maintenance, molecular movement, energy |
| 5.2 Nutrition | 5.2.1 autotrophic (photosynthesis); 5.2.2 heterotrophic; 5.2.3 how organisms obtain food (Amoeba, Paramecium); 5.2.4 human nutrition |
| 5.3 Respiration | aerobic, anaerobic; human respiratory system; plants |
| 5.4 Transportation | 5.4.1 in humans — heart, blood vessels, platelets, lymph; 5.4.2 in plants — xylem, phloem |
| 5.5 Excretion | 5.5.1 in humans — kidneys, nephron, dialysis; 5.5.2 in plants |

> Hook: A sleeping cat looks completely still. How do we know it is alive? Even asleep, molecules are moving inside it — it breathes, its heart pumps, its cells repair themselves. **Life processes** are the maintenance jobs that keep a living body running, even when it seems to do nothing.

Living structures are highly organised, and the environment tends to break order down. So bodies must constantly **repair and maintain** themselves — which needs **energy** from food (nutrition), oxygen to release that energy (respiration), a delivery network (transportation) and a way to remove harmful wastes (excretion). In single-celled organisms all of this happens across the cell surface; in large multicellular organisms, specialised tissues and organs are needed because diffusion alone is too slow.

check.q: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen needs of a large multicellular organism like a human?
options: Most cells are far from the surface, and diffusion over long distances is too slow
check.why: In a large body most cells are not in direct contact with air, and diffusion over such distances would be far too slow, so specialised breathing and transport systems are needed.

sections.md:
### 5.2.1 Autotrophic nutrition — photosynthesis
Green plants (and some bacteria) make their own food from CO₂ and water using sunlight, in the presence of **chlorophyll**:
> 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → (chlorophyll, sunlight) → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O

Three events: (i) absorption of light by chlorophyll; (ii) conversion of light energy to chemical energy and **splitting of water** into hydrogen and oxygen; (iii) **reduction of CO₂** to carbohydrates. These need not happen one immediately after another — **desert plants** take in CO₂ at night (when stomata can open without too much water loss) and store it as an intermediate, using it in the day.

Extra glucose is stored as **starch**.

**Stomata:** tiny pores on leaves for gas exchange, opened and closed by **guard cells**. Guard cells swell when water flows in (pore opens) and shrink when they lose water (pore closes). Plants close stomata when CO₂ isn’t needed, to reduce water loss.

**Activity 5.1 — chlorophyll is needed:** a potted plant with variegated leaves (green and white patches) is kept in darkness for three days (to destarch), then in sunlight. A leaf is boiled in alcohol (to remove chlorophyll), then tested with **iodine**: only the parts that were **green** turn blue-black (starch present).

**Activity 5.2 — CO₂ is needed:** two destarched plants under bell jars, one with **potassium hydroxide** (absorbs CO₂). After sunlight, only the leaf from the jar without KOH shows starch.

Plants also take **nitrogen, phosphorus, iron, magnesium** from soil; nitrogen as nitrates/nitrites or from bacteria.

### 5.2.2–5.2.3 Heterotrophic nutrition
Organisms that depend on others. Types: break down food outside the body and absorb it (fungi such as bread mould, yeast, mushrooms — **saprotrophic**); take in whole food and digest inside (humans, cows); derive nutrition from a living host without killing it (**parasites** — Cuscuta/amarbel, ticks, lice, tapeworms).

- **Amoeba** engulfs food using temporary finger-like **pseudopodia**, forming a **food vacuole**; food is digested inside and the undigested remains are thrown out at the surface.
- **Paramecium** has a definite shape; **cilia** sweep food to a specific spot, the oral groove.

options: To remove chlorophyll so the colour change is visible
check.why: Alcohol dissolves the green chlorophyll; a decolourised leaf lets you clearly see where iodine turns blue-black.

sections.md:
The alimentary canal is a long tube from **mouth to anus**, with regions specialised for different jobs.

| Region | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Mouth** | Teeth crush food; tongue mixes it; **saliva** contains **salivary amylase**, which breaks starch into simple sugar |
| **Oesophagus** | **Peristalsis** — rhythmic muscle contractions push food along the whole gut |
| **Stomach** | Gastric glands release **hydrochloric acid** (acidic medium, kills germs), **pepsin** (digests proteins) and **mucus** (protects the stomach lining from the acid). Excess acid causes ‘acidity’ |
| Sphincter | Muscle that releases food from the stomach in small amounts |
| **Small intestine** | Longest part (longer in herbivores, who digest cellulose; shorter in carnivores). Receives **bile** from the liver (makes food alkaline for pancreatic enzymes; **emulsifies fats** into small globules) and **pancreatic juice** (trypsin for proteins, lipase for emulsified fats, amylase). Intestinal glands finish the job: proteins → amino acids; carbohydrates → glucose; fats → fatty acids + glycerol |
| **Villi** | Finger-like projections greatly increase surface area; rich blood supply absorbs digested food |
| **Large intestine** | Absorbs more water; the rest is removed via the **anus**, regulated by the **anal sphincter** |

**Activity 5.3 — saliva digests starch:** two test tubes of starch solution; add saliva to one. After 20–30 minutes add iodine. The tube **with saliva** does not turn blue-black (starch digested); the other does.

**Did you know? — tooth decay:** bacteria acting on sugars produce acids that soften enamel (calcium phosphate). Bacterial cells with food particles form **dental plaque**. Brushing after eating removes plaque before acids form.

check.q: What is the role of bile in digestion?
options: Emulsifies fats and makes the food alkaline
check.why: Bile salts break large fat globules into small ones (emulsification) and bile makes food from the stomach alkaline so pancreatic enzymes can act.

sections.md:
Food (glucose) is broken down in steps to release energy. Step 1, in the **cytoplasm** of all cells: glucose (6-carbon) → **pyruvate** (3-carbon). Then:

| Pathway | Where | Products | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Absence of oxygen (**anaerobic**) | cytoplasm | ethanol + CO₂ + energy | **yeast** fermentation |
| Lack of oxygen | muscle cells | **lactic acid** + energy | muscle cramps after sudden heavy exercise |
| Presence of oxygen (**aerobic**) | **mitochondria** | CO₂ + water + much more energy | most cells |

The energy is stored in **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) — the ‘energy currency’ of the cell. Breaking a phosphate bond of ATP releases about **30.5 kJ/mol**, which powers muscle contraction, protein making and nerve impulses.

**Activity 5.4 — exhaled air has CO₂:** blow through lime water using a pipette, and pump ordinary air through another tube — the exhaled air turns lime water milky much faster.

**Activity 5.5 — yeast:** fruit juice with yeast in a sealed tube; the gas produced turns lime water milky (CO₂ from anaerobic respiration).

### Gas exchange in different organisms
- **Aquatic** animals use oxygen dissolved in water (much less than in air), so they breathe faster. Fish take water in through the mouth and force it past the **gills**.
- **Terrestrial** animals breathe air through thin, moist, protected surfaces.

### Human respiratory system
Nostrils (fine hairs and mucus filter air) → pharynx → **trachea** (held open by **rings of cartilage**) → **bronchi** → **bronchioles** → **alveoli**, balloon-like sacs with thin walls and a dense network of capillaries. Spread out, the alveoli would cover about **80 m²**.
- **Breathing in:** ribs lift and the **diaphragm** flattens; the chest cavity enlarges and air rushes in.
- Lungs always hold a **residual volume** of air, allowing continuous exchange.
- **Haemoglobin** in red blood cells carries oxygen (it has a very high affinity for it); **CO₂** is more soluble and is mainly carried dissolved in blood.

### Plants
Plants exchange gases through stomata and lenticels (stems) by diffusion. At night CO₂ is released; in the day, photosynthesis uses CO₂ and releases O₂ — the major exchange.

> Health note: smoking damages the cilia lining the airways and can lead to lung cancer — another reason to stay away from tobacco.

check.q: Where does aerobic respiration complete the breakdown of pyruvate?
check.why: In the presence of oxygen, pyruvate is broken down to CO₂ and water inside mitochondria, releasing much more energy.

sections.md:
### 5.4.1 Humans
**Blood** = fluid **plasma** (carries food, CO₂, nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form) + red blood cells (oxygen) + white blood cells + **platelets**.

**The heart** is a muscular organ about the size of a fist with **four chambers**. Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the **left atrium** → **left ventricle** (thick-walled, pumps to the whole body) → aorta. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the **right atrium** via the vena cava → **right ventricle** → lungs. **Valves** prevent backflow.

**Double circulation:** blood passes through the heart **twice** in each cycle (body → heart → lungs → heart → body). Keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate gives a highly efficient oxygen supply — needed by birds and mammals, which use lots of energy to keep body temperature constant.
- **Fish:** two-chambered heart; blood goes through the heart once per cycle (single circulation).
- **Amphibians and many reptiles:** three chambers; some mixing of blood.

**Blood pressure:** the force blood exerts on vessel walls. Systolic (ventricles contract) about 120 mm Hg; diastolic (ventricles relax) about 80 mm Hg. Measured with a **sphygmomanometer**. High blood pressure (hypertension) is caused by constricted arterioles and can rupture arteries — see a doctor for regular checks.

**Blood vessels:** **arteries** carry blood away from the heart, with thick elastic walls (high pressure); **veins** bring blood back, thinner walls, valves; **capillaries** are one cell thick — exchange happens here.

**Platelets** plug leaks by helping blood **clot** at an injury.

**Lymph (tissue fluid):** some plasma, proteins and blood cells escape from capillaries into intercellular spaces. Lymph is similar to plasma but colourless with less protein. It carries **digested fats** from the intestine and drains excess fluid back into the blood.

### 5.4.2 Plants
- **Xylem** carries water and minerals from roots upward. Root cells take up ions actively, creating a difference in concentration so water moves in from soil (root pressure, important at night). In the day, **transpiration** — loss of water vapour through stomata — creates a **suction pull** that draws water up even the tallest trees. Transpiration also helps **temperature regulation**.
- **Phloem** transports food (sucrose, amino acids) from leaves to other parts — **translocation**. It uses energy from ATP: sucrose is moved into phloem tissue, raising osmotic pressure so water enters, and this pressure moves material to areas of lower pressure. Phloem can carry food **up or down** as needed — in spring, sugar stored in roots or stems goes to buds.

check.q: Why do mammals and birds need separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood?
options: They have high energy needs to maintain constant body temperature
check.why: Warm-blooded animals constantly burn energy to keep their body temperature steady, so they need the efficient oxygen supply that a fully separated four-chambered heart provides.

sections.md:
**Excretion** is the removal of harmful metabolic nitrogenous wastes.

### 5.5.1 Humans
The excretory system: **two kidneys**, two **ureters**, the **urinary bladder** and the **urethra**.
- Each kidney has a huge number of filtration units called **nephrons**.
- A nephron begins with a cup-shaped **Bowman’s capsule** around a cluster of capillaries, the **glomerulus**, where blood is filtered.
- The filtrate contains glucose, amino acids, salts, water and urea. As it flows along the **tubule**, useful substances — glucose, amino acids, salts and a major amount of water — are **selectively reabsorbed**. How much water is reabsorbed depends on how much excess water the body has and how much waste must be dissolved.
- Urine collects in the bladder (whose muscular walls are under **nervous control**) and leaves through the urethra.

**Artificial kidney (haemodialysis):** if kidneys fail (because of infection, injury or restricted blood flow), poisonous wastes build up. In dialysis, blood is passed through long tubes with semi-permeable lining suspended in dialysing fluid of the same osmotic pressure as blood (but no nitrogenous waste). Wastes diffuse out; purified blood returns to the body. Unlike the kidney, **there is no reabsorption**. A normal adult filters about **180 litres** daily but excretes only about 1–2 litres of urine.

### 5.5.2 Plants
- Excess **oxygen** (from photosynthesis) and CO₂ leave through stomata.
- Excess **water** is lost by transpiration.
- Wastes are stored in **cellular vacuoles**, or in **leaves that fall off**.
- Some wastes are stored as **resins and gums**, especially in old xylem.
- Some are excreted into the soil around the roots.

> Did you know? Organ donation — including kidneys — can save lives. A person can live a healthy life with one kidney; donation is always a voluntary decision made with family and doctors.

check.why: Glucose, amino acids, salts and much water are reabsorbed, but most urea stays in the tubule and leaves in urine.

steps: Left ventricle pumps blood to the entire body
Right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs
workedExamples.answer: More force is needed to push blood around the whole body

summary: Life processes: nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion — for maintenance and repair.
Photosynthesis: light absorption, water splitting, CO₂ reduction; glucose stored as starch.
Stomata open/close via guard cells; desert plants fix CO₂ at night.
Heterotrophs: saprotrophs, holozoic, parasites; Amoeba uses pseudopodia, Paramecium cilia.

ATP is the energy currency of the cell.

Arteries, veins, capillaries; platelets clot blood; lymph carries fats.
Xylem moves water by transpiration pull; phloem translocates food using ATP.

rd-school-c10-science-a.ch6-control-and-.title: Control and Coordination
rd-school-c10-science-a.ch6-control-and-.subtitle: Why your hand jerks off a hot tawa before you even feel the pain — nerves, brain, hormones and plant movements

sections.md:
A fast bowler releases the ball at around 145 km/h. It reaches the batter in roughly 0.4 seconds. In that sliver of time the batter's eyes track the ball, the brain judges line and length, and dozens of muscles in the legs, back, arms and wrists fire in exactly the right order to play a cover drive. Nothing jerks, nothing is late. This is **control and coordination**.

The chapter opens with a simple observation: living things *move*, and much of that movement is a response to some change around them. A plant bends towards the window. A cat freezes when it hears a sound. A child pulls her hand back from a candle flame. Even movements that look automatic — a seedling pushing up through soil, the heart beating — are carefully regulated.

Any change in the environment to which an organism responds is a **stimulus** (plural: stimuli): light, heat, cold, sound, smell, taste, touch, pressure, gravity, chemicals. The reaction is a **response**. If movements in response to stimuli were random, the organism would be in trouble: a hand moving away from fire must move *away*, not toward it, and must move *fast*.

Multicellular organisms therefore use specialised tissues to provide control and coordination:

- Animals use two systems: the fast **nervous system** (electrical and chemical signals along nerves) and the slower **endocrine (hormonal) system** (chemicals carried in blood).
- Plants have no nervous or muscular tissue, so they use **chemical signals (plant hormones)** and changes in cell water content or growth.

In this read we follow the NCERT order: (1) the nervous system in animals — neurons, reflex actions, the human brain, protection of nervous tissue, and how nerves cause muscles to act; (2) coordination in plants — immediate responses and growth movements; (3) hormones in animals.

> **Did you know?** The fastest nerve fibres in your body conduct impulses at about 100 metres per second — quicker than a cricket ball and roughly as fast as a racing car.
keyTerms: Stimulus — a change in surroundings an organism responds to
Response — the reaction to a stimulus
Coordination — working of different organs together in a controlled way

check.q: Which pair of systems provides control and coordination in animals?
check.why: Animals coordinate their activities through the fast nervous system and the slower, longer-lasting hormonal (endocrine) system.

sections.h: 6.1 Animals — the nervous system: receptors and neurons
sections.md:
Information from the environment is detected by **receptors** — specialised tips of nerve cells, usually located in our sense organs:

| Sense organ | Receptors detect |
|---|---|
| Eyes | light (photoreceptors) |
| Inner ear | sound and balance (phonoreceptors) |
| Nose | smell (olfactory receptors) |
| Tongue | taste (gustatory receptors) |
| Skin | touch, pressure, heat, cold, pain (thermoreceptors etc.) |

### The neuron
The **neuron (nerve cell)** is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It has three main parts:

1. **Dendrites** — short, branched extensions of the cell body. Information is acquired here: a **chemical reaction** at the dendrite tip sets off an **electrical impulse**.
2. **Cell body (cyton)** — contains the nucleus and cytoplasm; the impulse passes from dendrite to cell body.
3. **Axon** — a long fibre carrying the impulse away from the cell body to its far end. Many axons are wrapped in an insulating **myelin sheath**, which speeds up conduction.

### The synapse — the gap that is crossed chemically
At the end of the axon, the electrical impulse triggers the release of certain **chemicals (neurotransmitters)**. These chemicals diffuse across a tiny gap called the **synapse** and start a similar electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. In this way the message hops from neuron to neuron. A similar synapse allows delivery of impulses from neurons to other cells, such as **muscle cells or glands**.

So the pathway is always one-way: **dendrite → cell body → axon → nerve ending → synapse → next cell**. It cannot go backwards because only axon endings release the chemicals and only the next cell has the receiving sites.

### Types of neurons by job
- **Sensory neurons** carry impulses from receptors to the brain or spinal cord.
- **Motor neurons** carry impulses from the brain or spinal cord to **effectors** (muscles and glands).
- **Relay (inter) neurons** connect sensory and motor neurons inside the spinal cord and brain.

Nervous tissue is thus a well-organised network of neurons specialised for conducting information via electrical impulses from one part of the body to another.

sections.md:
Touch a hot tawa and your hand flies back before you even think *"hot!"*. Get dust in your eye and you blink. These are **reflex actions** — sudden, automatic, involuntary responses to stimuli, done without conscious thinking.

Why do we need them? If the message about heat had to travel all the way to the thinking part of the brain, be processed, and a decision sent back, the hand could be burnt. Thinking is complex and slow. So the body has a shortcut.

### The reflex arc
The nerves that detect heat are connected to the nerves that move the muscles of the arm in a simple, quick way. This connection — detecting the signal and responding to it — usually happens in the **spinal cord**. The pathway is called a **reflex arc**:

**Receptor (skin) → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (arm muscle)**

Information still reaches the brain too: the input nerves continue up the spinal cord, so a moment later you *feel* the pain and know what happened. But the action has already been done.

Why have reflex arcs evolved? In many animals there is very little complex 'thinking' at all; reflex arcs in such animals may be the main way of responding. Even with complex brains developed later, reflex arcs remain efficient for quick responses and continue to be valuable.

**Examples of reflexes:** sneezing, coughing, blinking, knee-jerk, pulling the hand away from a pin or flame, watering of the mouth at the smell of food (salivation), the pupil shrinking in bright light.

**Activity idea (from the textbook type):** sit with your legs crossed and gently tap just below the kneecap — the lower leg kicks up by itself. That is the knee-jerk reflex, run by the spinal cord.

sections.md:
Reflexes are not the only thing the nervous system does. We also *think*, *plan*, *decide* and do **voluntary** actions like writing, talking or moving a chair. Here the brain is in charge.

The human nervous system has two parts:
- **Central nervous system (CNS):** the **brain** and the **spinal cord**. They receive information from all parts of the body and integrate it.
- **Peripheral nervous system (PNS):** the nerves connecting the CNS to the rest of the body — **cranial nerves** arising from the brain and **spinal nerves** arising from the spinal cord.

The brain is the main coordinating centre. It has three major regions:

### Fore-brain
The main **thinking** part. It has regions that receive sensory impulses from various receptors — separate areas specialised for hearing, smell, sight and so on. Separate areas of association interpret this sensory information by putting it together with information from other receptors and with what is already stored. Based on this, a decision is made about how to respond, and the information is passed to the **motor areas** that control voluntary muscles (e.g. our leg muscles). The **cerebrum** is the largest part. The fore-brain also has a centre associated with **hunger** (and feeling full) — the hypothalamus region.

### Mid-brain
Controls many **involuntary** actions, such as reflex movements of the head, neck and eyes in response to light and sound, and changes in pupil size.

### Hind-brain
Also controls involuntary actions. It has three parts:
- **Pons** — helps regulate breathing.
- **Medulla (medulla oblongata)** — controls blood pressure, salivation, vomiting, and involuntary actions like heart-beat.
- **Cerebellum** — responsible for the **precision of voluntary actions and maintaining posture and balance** of the body. Walking in a straight line, riding a bicycle, picking up a pencil — the cerebellum makes them smooth.

Not all involuntary actions are reflexes in the spinal-cord sense: the beating of the heart or salivation at the sight of food are controlled by the hind-brain and mid-brain. A thought experiment the textbook raises: think of something you do *without* thinking (breathing, digesting) and something you *decide* (walking to the window). Different parts of the brain govern each.

sections.md:
Something as delicate and important as the brain needs very careful protection.

- The **brain** sits inside a bony box, the **cranium (skull)**. Inside the box, the brain is wrapped in membranes and cushioned by a **fluid-filled balloon** (cerebrospinal fluid) that absorbs shocks.
- The **spinal cord** is protected by the **vertebral column (backbone)** — a chain of ring-like bones, the vertebrae, through which the cord runs.

This is why helmets matter on a two-wheeler: the fluid cushion handles a nod or a small bump, but not the sudden stop of a 40 km/h fall.

> **Did you know?** Your brain uses roughly a fifth of your body's resting energy, even though it is only about 2% of body mass.

sections.h: 6.1.4 How does the nervous tissue cause action?
sections.md:
So far: receptors pick up information, neurons carry it, the brain or spinal cord decides. The final step is to *do* something — usually move a muscle. How does a nerve make a muscle move?

When a nerve impulse reaches the muscle, the **muscle fibre moves**. Muscle cells move by **changing their shape so that they shorten**. Muscle cells contain **special proteins** that change both their shape and their arrangement in the cell in response to nervous electrical impulses. When this happens, new arrangements of these proteins give the muscle cells a shorter form — the muscle **contracts**.

Remember the types of muscle from Class 9:
- **Voluntary (skeletal, striated) muscles** — under our control, e.g. arm and leg muscles.
- **Involuntary (smooth) muscles** — e.g. in the gut and blood vessels.
- **Cardiac muscle** — heart; involuntary.

### Limitations of electrical signalling
The textbook points out that electrical impulses are an excellent way of sending information quickly, but they have limits:
1. They reach **only those cells connected by nervous tissue**, not every cell of the body.
2. Once a cell generates and transmits an impulse, it needs **some time to reset** before it can send another — so cells cannot continually create and send impulses.

That is why most multicellular organisms also use **chemical communication** — hormones — which can reach every cell through the blood and act over longer periods. We meet plant chemicals next, and animal hormones after that.

check.q: Muscle cells shorten because:
options: Special proteins in them change shape and arrangement
check.why: A nerve impulse causes special muscle proteins to rearrange, giving the cell a shorter form, which is contraction.

sections.md:
Plants have neither a nervous system nor muscles. Yet they respond to stimuli. Touch the leaves of a *chhui-mui* (touch-me-not, *Mimosa pudica*) and they fold up and droop. A seed planted upside-down still sends its root downward and its shoot upward. Plants show two kinds of movement:

1. **Movements independent of growth** — fast, immediate responses (like the sensitive plant).
2. **Movements dependent on growth** — slow, directional growth (like a shoot bending toward light).

### 6.2.1 Immediate response to stimulus
In the sensitive plant, the leaves respond to touch very quickly, with no growth involved. But how does the plant detect touch, and how does the message travel without nerves?

- The plant uses **electrical-chemical means** to convey information from cell to cell, but unlike animals there is **no specialised tissue** for conducting it.
- To move, the cells **change shape by changing the amount of water** in them. When cells at the base of the leaf (the pulvinus) lose water, they become limp (lose turgor), and the leaf folds and droops.

So animal muscle moves by protein rearrangement; plant cells move by water movement — a lovely compare-and-contrast question for exams.

### 6.2.2 Movement due to growth
Some plants like the pea plant climb using **tendrils**. Tendrils are sensitive to touch: when they come in contact with a support, the part of the tendril in contact grows **slower** than the part away from it. The faster-growing outer side makes the tendril curl around the support.

More commonly, plants respond to stimuli slowly by growing in a particular direction. Because this growth is directional, it looks like movement. Directional growth movements are called **tropisms** (towards the stimulus = positive; away = negative):

| Tropism | Stimulus | Shoot | Root |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phototropism | light | towards (+) | away (−) |
| Geotropism (gravitropism) | gravity | away / upward (−) | towards / downward (+) |
| Hydrotropism | water | — | towards (+) |
| Chemotropism | chemicals | pollen tube grows towards ovule (+) | — |
| Thigmotropism | touch | tendrils coil around support | — |

**Activity type:** fill a conical flask with water, cover the neck with wire mesh, put two or three freshly germinated bean seeds on the mesh, and keep it in a box open on one side facing a window. In two or three days, the shoots bend towards light and the roots away from it. Turn the flask so the shoots face away from the light — in a few days the old parts stay put but **new growth bends again toward light**.

sections.h: Plant hormones — the chemical messengers of plants
sections.md:
How does a shoot 'know' which side the light is on? Through **plant hormones (phytohormones)** — chemicals that coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment. They are made in one part of the plant and diffuse to the area of action.

### Auxin and the bending shoot
When growing plants detect light, a hormone called **auxin**, synthesised at the **shoot tip**, helps the cells to grow longer. When light comes from one side, auxin **diffuses towards the shady side** of the shoot. This higher concentration of auxin stimulates the cells on the shaded side to grow longer than those on the lit side. The shoot therefore **bends towards light**.

### The four other hormones you must know
| Hormone | Main role |
|---|---|
| **Auxin** | cell elongation at shoot tip; phototropism |
| **Gibberellins** | help in growth of the stem (stem elongation) |
| **Cytokinins** | promote cell division; present in high concentration in areas of rapid division such as fruits and seeds |
| **Abscisic acid (ABA)** | inhibits growth; causes wilting of leaves; called the 'stress hormone' |

Auxin, gibberellins and cytokinins are **growth promoters**; abscisic acid is a **growth inhibitor**. A plant balances them — e.g. ABA helps close stomata in drought, slowing water loss.

**Exam tip — compare animal and plant coordination:**

- Animals: nervous + hormonal; specialised conducting tissue; muscles contract by proteins; fast.
- Plants: hormonal + electrical-chemical cell-to-cell; no specialised tissue; movement by water change or growth; mostly slow.
keyTerms: Tropism — directional growth movement in response to a stimulus
Auxin — shoot-tip hormone causing cell elongation
Abscisic acid — growth-inhibiting stress hormone

check.q: When light falls on a shoot from the left, auxin collects on the:
options: Left (lit) side, so the shoot bends right
Right (shaded) side, so the shoot bends left
check.why: Auxin diffuses to the shaded side, making those cells elongate more, so the shoot curves toward the light.

sections.md:
Picture a squirrel that suddenly meets a dog. Its heart races, it breathes faster, and it is ready either to fight or to run. Many tissues all over its body must be prepared at once — something nerves alone can't easily do. This is done by **adrenaline**.

### Adrenaline — the emergency hormone
Adrenaline is secreted by the **adrenal glands** (on top of the kidneys) directly into the **blood** and carried to different parts of the body. Its target organs include the heart: **the heart beats faster**, supplying more oxygen to muscles. Blood supply to the digestive system and skin is **reduced** because small arteries around them contract — diverting blood to skeletal muscles. **Breathing rate increases** because the diaphragm and rib muscles contract. All these prepare the animal to deal with the situation.

These animal hormones are part of the **endocrine system**, the second way of control and coordination. **Endocrine glands** are ductless; they pour secretions straight into blood.

### The glands you must know
| Gland | Location | Hormone | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hypothalamus | brain | releasing hormones | regulates pituitary secretions (e.g. growth hormone releasing factor) |
| Pituitary | below brain | growth hormone, and others | regulates growth and development; controls other glands ('master gland') |
| Thyroid | neck | **thyroxin** | regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism for growth |
| Pancreas | below stomach | **insulin** | lowers blood sugar level |
| Adrenal | above kidneys | **adrenaline** | prepares body for emergency |
| Testes (male) | — | **testosterone** | changes at puberty in males |
| Ovaries (female) | — | **oestrogen** | development of female organs; regulates menstrual cycle |

### Iodised salt and goitre
Iodine is necessary for the thyroid to make **thyroxin**. If iodine is deficient in the diet, we may suffer from **goitre** — a swollen neck. That is why iodised salt is recommended and sold across India.

### Growth hormone
If there is a deficiency of growth hormone in childhood, it leads to **dwarfism**; excess leads to **gigantism**.

### Puberty
During puberty (around 10–12 years onwards) many changes occur because of the secretion of **testosterone** in males and **oestrogen** in females.

### Insulin and diabetes
If insulin is not secreted in proper amounts, the sugar level in the blood rises, causing many harmful effects — this is **diabetes**. Many diabetics are treated with insulin injections, under a doctor's care.

### Feedback mechanisms
How is the right amount of a hormone released? Timing and amount are regulated by **feedback mechanisms**. For example, if the sugar level in blood rises, it is detected by the cells of the pancreas, which respond by producing more insulin. As blood sugar falls, insulin secretion is reduced. The system corrects itself — like a fridge thermostat.

sections.h: Nerves vs hormones — putting the chapter together
sections.md:
| Feature | Nervous control | Hormonal control |
|---|---|---|
| Messenger | electrical impulse + chemical at synapse | chemical (hormone) |
| Route | along nerve fibres | through blood |
| Speed | very fast (milliseconds) | slower (seconds to days) |
| Effect lasts | short | longer |
| Reach | only cells connected to nerves | any cell with receptors |
| Example | pulling hand from flame | growth at puberty |

The two systems work together. The **hypothalamus** in the brain links them: it is nervous tissue that also makes releasing hormones that tell the pituitary what to do. In the squirrel's emergency, nerves signal the adrenal glands, which then flood the body with adrenaline.

A tidy flow to remember the whole chapter:

**Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → CNS (spinal cord for reflex, brain for voluntary) → motor neuron → effector (muscle/gland) → response**; with hormones running in parallel through the blood for slower, wider, longer-lasting control. In plants: **stimulus → hormone (auxin etc.) or water change → growth or movement**.

> **Did you know?** Sunflower buds track the sun from east to west during the day — a growth-driven movement in the stem — and the mature heads mostly face east.

workedExamples.q: Trace the path of the message when you step on a sharp stone and lift your foot.
steps: Pain receptors in the skin of the sole detect the stimulus.
A sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord.
A relay neuron in the spinal cord passes it directly to a motor neuron.
The motor neuron carries the impulse to the leg muscles (effector).
Muscles contract and the foot lifts; meanwhile a signal travels up to the brain, so you feel pain a moment later.
workedExamples.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → leg muscle: a reflex arc.

workedExamples.q: A potted plant is kept near a window for a week and its shoot bends toward the window. Explain.
steps: Auxin is made at the shoot tip.
Light falls on one side; auxin diffuses to the shaded side.
Cells on the shaded side elongate more.
Unequal growth curves the shoot toward light: positive phototropism.
workedExamples.answer: Unequal auxin-driven cell elongation causes the shoot to bend toward light.

workedExamples.q: Why is blood supply to the digestive system reduced when adrenaline is released?
steps: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight.
Small arteries around the gut and skin contract.
Blood is diverted to skeletal muscles that need oxygen and glucose for action.
workedExamples.answer: To divert more blood and oxygen to muscles during an emergency.

workedExamples.q: Identify the brain region: (a) maintaining balance on a moving bus; (b) vomiting; (c) thinking about a maths problem; (d) pupil size changing in sunlight.

summary: Control and coordination in animals are provided by the nervous and endocrine systems.
Receptors in sense organs detect stimuli; the neuron (dendrite, cell body, axon) is the unit of nervous tissue.
An impulse is electrical in a neuron and chemical across a synapse; it travels one way.
Reflex actions are quick involuntary responses routed through the spinal cord via a reflex arc.
CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = cranial and spinal nerves.
Fore-brain: thinking, sensory and motor areas, hunger; mid-brain and hind-brain: involuntary actions.
Hind-brain: pons (breathing), medulla (BP, salivation, vomiting), cerebellum (balance, precision).
Brain is protected by skull and fluid; spinal cord by vertebral column.
Muscles contract when special proteins rearrange in response to impulses.
Plants respond by immediate (water change) and growth movements (tropisms).
Auxin causes phototropism; gibberellins stem growth; cytokinins cell division; abscisic acid inhibits growth.
Endocrine glands release hormones into blood: thyroxin, growth hormone, insulin, adrenaline, testosterone, oestrogen.
Iodine deficiency → goitre; insulin deficiency → diabetes; growth hormone imbalance → dwarfism/gigantism.
Feedback mechanisms regulate the timing and amount of hormone release.

Muscle or gland that carries out a response
